messages.subject: Allele Estimates for RIL population
parts:
Dr. Broman-

I am a PhD student conducting a linkage mapping study in soybean. I am encountering discrepancies with allele estimates from the 4 QTL I identified using the scanone function, and the estimates ultimately derived from the fitqtl function. This is an F6 derived RIL set. 320 RILs were phenotyped. I performed selective genotyping of the top and bottom 20% tails (so, 128 lines total genotyped). Genotyping-by-sequencing was used to generate the markers. I trimmed the markers down to a very high-quality number of 1400 markers. It is my understanding that the effect of the marker should be one-half the difference of the phenotypic mean of each marker class, (AA-BB/2). This shoudl be close to what the fitqtl function outputs. As shown in the table below, this is considerable difference between the two methods. I am very cognizant that allele estimates are usually always poor, due to things such as population used and the Beavis effect. I don't put much stock into either of the estimates, but was confused why there was so much discrepancy.

Some confounding factors I think (but may be wrong) that are causing this:

-The complete set of RILs was not genotyped, so selective genotypic may be causing some bias. 
-Disproportionate numbers of RILs in each class (i.e for Marker1, 50 RILs have the 'A' allele while 78 have the 'B' allele. Similar situations for the other 3 markers.


I have attached what I think is relevant code. I appreciate any thoughts. Thanks


##Relevant code

outfour.imp <- scanone(mapthis, pheno.col=2, method="ehk")
summary(outfour.imp, threshold=3.11) ##the permutation threshold was 3.11 when I ran it
chr=summary(outfour.imp, threshold=3)$chr
pos=summary(outfour.imp, threshold=3)$pos
qtl=makeqtl(mapthis,chr=chr,pos=pos,what="draws")
out.fq <- fitqtl(mapthis,pheno.col=2,qtl=qtl,formula=y~Q1+Q2+Q3+Q4,get.ests=TRUE,method="imp")

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Allele Estimates for RIL population
parts:
I think fitqtl is working fine for RIL by selfing. I tried it out (code at https://gist.github.com/kbroman/9939651) and it works as I'd expect.

There are a number of ways in which things could be going wrong.

1. Is the cross type correct?

class(mycross)[1] # should say "riself"

If you have the cross as a backcross ("bc") then the estimated effects will be the difference between the two phenotype averages, rather than half the difference.

2. Did you include the lines with phenotypes but no genotypes?

With selective genotyping, you really need to include all lines. If you consider just the genotyped lines, you'll get severely biased estimates of the QTL effects. Consider Figure 4.15 in the R/qtl book (page 99); pdf at http://www.rqtl.org/book/rqtlbook_ch04.pdf

If you include the ungenotyped lines, the direct estimates of the phenotype differences will be distorted relative to what fitqtl gives you, as the ungenotyped individuals would be omitted in the direct estimates but not in fitqtl. Still, fitqtl is going to give potentially terrible estimates: Haley-Knott regression behaves poorly in the case of selective genotyping, and imputation will need a very large number of imputations (n.draws) to handle the complete uncertainty you have about the genotypes of those middle lines.

karl
